
==============================================================================
                      ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING THEY KNOW                    
==============================================================================

   You are one person, dropped into a pre-industrial society, carrying the
   knowledge of how modern technology works and none of the industry that makes
   it. Knowing how a thing works is free. Building it is not: it costs your own
   hours, other people's hours, money, materials, and years you do not get
   back.

   You arrive alone. No employees, no slaves, nobody who owes you anything, and
   about enough money to eat for a few months.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHERE, AND WHEN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   1) The Later Han Empire, 100
      Rome's exact contemporary and ahead of it in metallurgy, agriculture and
      bureaucracy. Cast iron for five centuries already, the seed drill, the
      moldboard plough, paper in the year 105, water-powered blast bellows in 31
      AD.
      58,000,000 people   state capacity 0.90   prices 0.75x Rome

   2) The Roman Empire under Trajan, 100
      Peak territorial extent, sound currency, superb civil engineering, an
      economy resting on slavery, and an elite that despises manual work.
      65,000,000 people   state capacity 0.85   prices 1.00x Rome

   3) Scandinavia in the Viking age, 900
      Small population, no state to speak of, superb shipbuilding and ironworking,
      and the best long-range mobility in Europe. The opposite problem from Rome:
      nobody will stop you, and nobody can fund you either.
      1,500,000 people   state capacity 0.15   prices 1.40x Rome

   4) England under Edward I, 1300
      Watermills and windmills everywhere, a real legal system, chartered towns,
      universities, the horse collar, the crank, the mechanical clock arriving,
      and about to be hit by the worst demographic catastrophe in European
      history.
      4,500,000 people   state capacity 0.60   prices 1.10x Rome

   5) The Mexica Triple Alliance, 1500
      A large, dense, literate, well-administered state with monumental
      construction, chinampa agriculture that outyields anything in Europe, and no
      draught animals, no iron, no wheel in practical use.
      5,000,000 people   state capacity 0.80   prices 0.80x Rome

   Which one? [1-5, or q to leave] 
==============================================================================
   THE ROMAN EMPIRE UNDER TRAJAN, 100
==============================================================================

   You come to on the Ostia road in the eighteenth year of Domitian's calendar,
   except Domitian is four years dead and nobody has corrected the milestone.
   It is the second consulship of Trajan. Rome is at its greatest extent and
   its most confident: the roads are the best in the world, the water arrives
   on schedule, the courts sit, the grain fleet comes in from Alexandria, and
   sixty-five million people are governed by men who genuinely believe the
   arrangement is permanent.

   WHAT YOU CAN SEE
   Concrete that sets under water. Glass windows. Surgical instruments a modern
   surgeon would recognise. Water-mills in banks of sixteen. A postal service
   that outruns anything Europe will have again for fourteen hundred years. And
   no mechanical clock, no printing, no spectacles, no chimney, no stirrup, no
   zero.

   WHAT IS MISSING
   Not the ideas. The instruments. Nobody can measure a temperature, hold a
   tolerance, sustain a vacuum, or purify anything. Every single thing you know
   how to build waits behind those four.

   WHAT IS COMING, AND ONLY YOU KNOW IT
   Sixty-five good years, then the Antonine plague. A century after that, the
   currency is debased to a tenth and the frontier stops holding. You know the
   dates. Nobody else does.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   FOG OF WAR. With it on you see what you have built, what you could begin
   today as a one-line summary, and things you have heard of but cannot yet
   start. You cannot see where anything leads. With it off you can see the
   whole tree and plan a route through it.

   Fog of war? [Y/n] 
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHAT YOU ARRIVED WITH
      destitute              0 den
         the clothes you stand in. You must earn your first meal.
      poor_scholar         400 den
         DEFAULT. A few months' subsistence, a knife, a lens, a codex of notes. About
         what a working teacher has.
      artisan            1,200 den
         enough to rent a workshop and buy a first set of tools.
      merchant           4,000 den
         a modest trading capital. You can fund one real venture.
      rich_merchant     20,000 den
         wealthy but well under the equestrian census of 100,000.
      equestrian       100,000 den
         the equestrian census exactly. Conspicuous.
      absurd         1,000,000 den
         four senatorial fortunes in unminted gold. It used to make things worse and
         no longer does: once money can be converted into protection and into sunk
         mines, wealth helps. What it does NOT do is make you a magician: a million
         denarii buys perhaps a tenth off the time, not a different game. What money
         changes most is the OPENING - the first fifty years, where a poor founder is
         choosing between eating and building.

   Which? [destitute/poor_scholar/artisan/merchant/rich_merchant/equestrian/absurd] 
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   MORTALITY. By default the founder does not age, which measures the tree
   rather than a lifespan lottery. Turned on, you get one human life and
   everything you have not made permanent dies with you. The premise of the
   whole game is that one is the honest number.

   Let the founder age and die? [y/N] 
==============================================================================
   Starting now. Progress is written to this file after every command, so you
   can stop any time - close the terminal, anything - and come back to exactly
   where you left off with:

      python3 rome/sim/simulator.py play --session /root/.rome-saves/rome_100ad_34.json


   You arrive in 100 AD with 400 denarii and nothing else: no employees, no
   slaves, and nobody who owes you anything. What you have is everything you
   know.

   Type commands in plain words. The five to start with are 'state' (where you
   stand), 'available' (what you could begin today), 'why <name>' (what a thing
   is for and what it costs), 'start <name>' (begin it) and 'step' (let a year
   pass). When something is FINISHED it earns nothing until you 'open' it.
   'stuck' says why you are not getting on; 'help' explains the rest; 'quit'
   leaves.

[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > help:
  what this is: You are one person, dropped into a pre-industrial society, carrying the knowledge of how modern technology works but none of the industry that makes it. You are playing The Roman Empire under Trajan, beginning in 100. Knowing how a thing works is free. Building it is not: it takes your own hours, other people's hours, money, materials, and years.
  how a turn works: You begin projects, then advance time. Nothing happens unless you make it. You are charged for food, rent and appearances every year whether or not you are building anything.
  what you are trying to do: Build point-contact transistor, before the horizon at 600. You know what it is and what it is for; what you cannot see is the road there, only the next step of it.
  you arrive alone: No employees, no slaves, nobody who owes you anything. Anyone who works for you is hired, taught, commissioned or bought. See help labour.
  the five you need first:
    state: where you stand
    available: what you could begin today
    why <id>: everything known about one thing
    start <id>: begin it
    step <years>: let time pass
  and the one rule that catches everybody: Finishing something earns you nothing. A concern earns when you 'open' it, and costs its upkeep only then too. ventures lists what you know how to run and have not opened.
  when you cannot see why you are not getting on: stuck
  how to send a command: One command per line, in plain words: "available", "step 5", "hire smith 2", "why fud_wheelbarrow". Pasting a JSON command works too, if you happen to have one.

[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > help:
  where it comes from: Your practice - the trade this society already had, which you can do from the first day - plus every concern you have OPENED, plus what your own workshop sells. money itemises all of it and the rows sum to the revenue above them.
  your practice pays less than the tree quotes: About a third: one person in a rented room is not an organised concern, and that gap does not close with time. Selling your hours for wages takes another bite, because you cannot be in two places.
  a concern you open starts small: It reaches its full figure over about three years.
  where it goes: Living and appearances, wages, the upkeep of what you are RUNNING, mines standing whether or not you work them, and interest on arrears.
  money costs money to hold: Living and appearances is about a sixtieth of your capital a year, on top of a subsistence floor and your household, plus a fixed sum for each rank you hold. In a patronage society a man visibly richer than he lives is suspected, and a man seeking standing must spend on it. An idle million bleeds about fifteen thousand a year doing nothing, which is why money sitting still is money going backwards.
  what you can buy: help economy
  debt: You may spend past what you have, as far as somebody will lend you and no further. Arrears cost interest.

[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > help:
  the ledger: money itemises what comes in and what goes out, including where the income comes from
  buy forest: buy forest 100 hectares of coppice, which is where charcoal comes from
  buy nitre: buy nitre 20,000 square metres of nitre bed. Saltpetre is made, not mined, and nothing else supplies it.
  buy mine: buy mine coal 500 tonnes a year of your own workings; it takes years to sink, and it costs to keep standing whether or not you use it. ASK THE PRICE FIRST with quote mine coal 500, and close it with close coal. Materials: coal, iron, copper, lead, tin, silver, gold
  buy slaves: buy slaves 5. This is available because it was the ordinary condition of production in most of these societies, and a model that hides it lies about the cost of everything.
  manumit: buy manumit 5 frees people you hold. They then work better, and it is the decent thing.
  debt: You may spend past what you have, as far as somebody will lend you and no further. Arrears cost interest.

TREE, only what you are RUNNING earns anything or costs anything. 'open
<id>' starts one, 'mothball <id>' stops it, and you keep the knowledge
either way.

[100 AD | 400 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 0 | rep 5] > Controlled experiment, hypothesis, replication, publication  [scientific_method]
==============================================================================
tier 0, foundation, confidence C

The hard part is not stating it, it is displacing Aristotelian authority.
Risk is high because the failure mode is cultural, not technical. Multiplier
on every research node thereafter. Contradicting Aristotle and Galen in
public is a social act before it is an intellectual one, and their defenders
hold the chairs, the patronage and the medical guild. Expect organised
opposition, not curiosity. (Needs no standing: writing down zero, or running
a controlled experiment, is something a nobody can do. What standing buys is
being BELIEVED, which is reputation, not a prerequisite.)

COST: 230 den total  (100 labour + 0 materials + 100 capital, then x1 your civ, x1 distance, x1 scarcity, x1.15 opposition, x1 prices)
YOUR HOURS: 350     CALENDAR FLOOR: 2 years     FAILURE RISK: 20%

tier 0, foundation, confidence C

Buy books, a house, clothes, a literate freed or hired secretary, and a
reputation for piety (in Rome this is specifically the Alexandrian
physician-philosopher persona; every society has its own version of a
scholar-notable it will not look at twice: a monk or clerk under any

or lawspeaker in Scandinavia). Reduces all future suspicion.

[104 AD | -2024 den | you:2000 hr | sch 0 art 2 | rep 18] > help:
  commands:
    state: where you stand; add full:true for every field
    available: what you could begin today, summarised by subject; add subject, find, afford, limit/offset, or all:true
    why <id>: everything known about one thing
    start <id>: begin work on something
    stop <id>: abandon it, losing what you have spent
    step <years>: let time pass
    money: the whole ledger: what comes in, what goes out
    quote <what>: what something would cost before you commit to it; so far quote mine coal 500
    close <material>: shut your own workings down and stop paying to keep them standing
    risk: what history is about to do to you, and what blunts it
    labour: who you employ and what trades exist here
    hire / fire / train / commission: see the labour topic
    buy: forest, nitre, mine, slaves, or manumit; see the economy topic
    work <trade> <hours>: do an ordinary job for ordinary pay
    bounty <id>: pay someone else to solve it instead
    open <id>: start actually running something you have worked out how to do; until you do, it earns nothing and costs nothing
    ventures: what you are running, and what you know how to run and have not opened
    mothball <id> / restore <id>: shut a finished work down, or reopen it
    bribe <amount>: spend money to reduce a scandal
    policy: every automatic behaviour, and a switch for each
    path <id>: not available under fog of war
    save <file> / load <file>: write or read a game
    help: this; add a topic
    quit: stop

  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.
switched on but cannot act right now:
  auto open: nothing to open with: opening a concern costs stock and premises

[114 AD | -1223 den | you:2000 hr | sch 3 art 4 | rep 24] > help:
  protection: How far your standing shields you when you produce an effect nobody can explain. It decides whether a strange result out of your workshop is read as learning or as sorcery, and it is the only thing money can buy here directly.
  what raises it: A patron, citizenship, a licensed collegium, land endowed in public, a school, and your reputation - and spending on advocacy and piety, which is what `bribe` does when you have no scandal to answer. Protection caps at 92% in total, and money is only 30 points of that however much you spend - a break tester read the 92 as the ceiling on bribery, offered a million, and stopped at the same 32% a hundred had bought. The rest has to be earned.
  what it does NOT protect you from: Eminence. Being too large is the one hazard no protection touches; see help eminence.
  where to watch it: state shows it under STANDING

[114 AD | -1223 den | you:2000 hr | sch 3 art 4 | rep 24] > help:
  eminence: The one hazard no patron, no bribe and no reputation protects you from, because it IS reputation. It rises with how well known you are and how visibly rich, it is multiplied by standing close to the throne, and past the danger line it rolls every year for your ruin. Sejanus was the most protected man in Rome until the morning he was not.
  what lowers it: One command does, and its price is real: withdraw halves your prominence now and gives up half the reputation you hold above what your work by itself is worth. Reputation here is your credit limit, your protection, the wages you must pay and the pace of your projects, so you cannot get small and stay grand - and you cannot do it twice in twelve years, because being seen to retire repeatedly is not retiring.
  what survives it: A wide, dispersed institution - academy_network makes the hazard itself smaller, and corpus_dispersed means what you know is in too many places to burn. Being merely rich and merely famous is the dangerous combination.
  and time helps: A city gets used to you. The longer you have been a fixture and the more of your work it has already seen, the less alarming the next thing is - the same familiarity that decays the alarm your work causes takes up to a third off this.
  if it lands: 45% of the time it is a confiscation and a forced retirement, 35% your patron is destroyed in somebody else's quarrel, and 20% it is the end of the run. `state` shows both figures.
  where to watch it: state shows it under STANDING

either way.

[235-284] Third century crisis
  Rome's baseline shifts in what this society values note that it is magic,
  not heterodoxy, that is criminal here, because the state has never before
  needed everyone to worship the same way. The Decian edict of 250 breaks
  that: for the first time, sacrifice to the emperor's genius is demanded
  empire-wide and certified in writing, a loyalty test with no precedent,
  followed by Valerian's edicts against Christians in 257-258. That is a real
  tightening of religious rigidity, not merely more of the old
  magic-suspicion, so it is modelled as its own small shift below rather than

[284-305] Diocletian's reforms and the Price Edict
  Diocletian came to power in 284 and rebuilt the state by making it much
  heavier. The tetrarchy of 293 gave the empire four courts to feed; the army
  was roughly doubled; the iugatio-capitatio assessment taxed land and heads
  together, often in kind, and needed a census machinery Rome had never had.
  The Edict on Maximum Prices of 301 fixed ceilings on more than a thousand
  goods and wages on pain of death, and Lactantius (De mortibus persecutorum
  7) says blood was shed over trifles until the law was quietly let die. The
  same decades made the collegia hereditary: a man's son inherited his trade
  and could not leave it, which is a direct constraint on anyone who wants to
  work at something new. That, and not the persecution of 303-311, is why how
  much trade is honoured falls here. The state also gets stronger and its
  favour correspondingly more decisive, which is the patronage shift.
  output factor: you take 90% of it (softened by your own roads)
    what would help: land and power of your own, and not depending on trade that a war can cut
    you could begin now: fin_marine_insurance (4,105, losses spread rather than borne), horse_collar (709.4, a step toward you feed yourself)
    crop_rotation is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: horse_collar
    school_founded is one of them, waiting on: this needs 2 other things you have not heard of yet, and you do not yet know what they are

[224 AD | 357654 den | you:2000 hr | sch 2 art 3 | rep 86] > Found the school (the Museum)  [school_founded]
===============================================
tier 1, institution, confidence C

The pivot of the entire game. Converts your hours into other people's hours
permanently. Every year of delay here costs more than any single technology.
Grants +4 scholars and +2 scholars/yr thereafter. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by
diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to
train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy
this down. OPTIONAL. Nothing in the technical tree requires it. It is simply
the highest-leverage thing you can spend money on, because it converts your
hours into other people's hours permanently. You may decline to found it and
hire craftsmen forever instead; the simulator will let you, and will show
you the cost.

COST: 11,500 den total  (2,000 labour + 0 materials + 8,000 capital, then x1 your civ, x1 distance, x1 scarcity, x1.15 opposition, x1 prices)

[224 AD | 357654 den | you:2000 hr | sch 2 art 3 | rep 86] > Buy, train and manumit a technical staff  [freedman_staff]
==========================================================
tier 1, institution, confidence C

Acquire, train and free a technical staff: buy or bind skilled workers,
teach them, release them from their obligation, then pay and keep them. A
freed worker who remains literate and paid transmits knowledge onward; a
coerced one does not. In Rome this is manumission of skilled slaves, who
retain an obligation to their former owner as patron and ran much of Roman
commerce; the Norse equivalent is working off a debt-thrall's bond.
Whichever form bondage takes where you are playing, this is both the ethical
and the efficient answer. Grants +8 artisans.

COST: 10,000 den total  (0 labour + 8,000 materials + 2,000 capital, then x1 your civ, x1 distance, x1 scarcity, x1 opposition, x1 prices)
YOUR HOURS: 900     CALENDAR FLOOR: 2 years     FAILURE RISK: 10%
STAFF NEEDED: 0 scholars, 0 artisans   (you have 3.5, 3.3)
MATERIALS: slave_skilled 8
UPKEEP: 1,400 den/yr     REVENUE: 0 den/yr

STATUS: CAN START NOW
PREREQUISITES (all met, and finished counts for ever): workshop_first
HOW MUCH RESTS ON THIS: a fair amount

[404 AD | 185038806 den | you:18722 hr | sch 6 art 28 | rep 99] > Czochralski single crystal growth and controlled doping  [single_crystal]
=========================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

Dip a seed into the melt and pull slowly while rotating. Grain boundaries
destroy carrier lifetime, so polycrystalline germanium will never make a
working transistor no matter how pure it is. Add the dopant to the melt in
weighed traces; this is where the analytical balance earns its keep two
centuries later.

[452 AD | 382134387 den | you:18673 hr | sch 23 art 245 | rep 82] > Czochralski single crystal growth and controlled doping  [single_crystal]
=========================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

Dip a seed into the melt and pull slowly while rotating. Grain boundaries
destroy carrier lifetime, so polycrystalline germanium will never make a
working transistor no matter how pure it is. Add the dopant to the melt in
weighed traces; this is where the analytical balance earns its keep two
centuries later.

[452 AD | 382134387 den | you:18673 hr | sch 23 art 245 | rep 82] > Diode, triode, and the first amplifier  [vacuum_tube]
=====================================================
tier 5, electrical, confidence B

Glass-to-metal seals need matched thermal expansion (Dumet wire) or they
crack; getters finish the vacuum after sealing. A working amplifier
transforms every instrument you own and is the practical precondition for
doing sensitive semiconductor measurements at all. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by
diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to
train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy
this down.

what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

[550 AD | 555215949 den | you:18633 hr | sch 26 art 379 | rep 96] > Czochralski single crystal growth and controlled doping  [single_crystal]
=========================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

Dip a seed into the melt and pull slowly while rotating. Grain boundaries
destroy carrier lifetime, so polycrystalline germanium will never make a
working transistor no matter how pure it is. Add the dopant to the melt in
weighed traces; this is where the analytical balance earns its keep two
centuries later.

==============================================================================
                      ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING THEY KNOW                    
==============================================================================

   You are one person, dropped into a pre-industrial society, carrying the
   knowledge of how modern technology works and none of the industry that makes
   it. Knowing how a thing works is free. Building it is not: it costs your own
   hours, other people's hours, money, materials, and years you do not get
   back.

   You arrive alone. No employees, no slaves, nobody who owes you anything, and
   about enough money to eat for a few months.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHERE, AND WHEN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   1) The Later Han Empire, 100
      Rome's exact contemporary and ahead of it in metallurgy, agriculture and
      bureaucracy. Cast iron for five centuries already, the seed drill, the
      moldboard plough, paper in the year 105, water-powered blast bellows in 31
      AD.
      58,000,000 people   state capacity 0.90   prices 0.75x Rome

   2) The Roman Empire under Trajan, 100
      Peak territorial extent, sound currency, superb civil engineering, an
      economy resting on slavery, and an elite that despises manual work.
      65,000,000 people   state capacity 0.85   prices 1.00x Rome

   3) Scandinavia in the Viking age, 900
      Small population, no state to speak of, superb shipbuilding and ironworking,
      and the best long-range mobility in Europe. The opposite problem from Rome:
      nobody will stop you, and nobody can fund you either.
      1,500,000 people   state capacity 0.15   prices 1.40x Rome

   4) England under Edward I, 1300
      Watermills and windmills everywhere, a real legal system, chartered towns,
      universities, the horse collar, the crank, the mechanical clock arriving,
      and about to be hit by the worst demographic catastrophe in European
      history.
      4,500,000 people   state capacity 0.60   prices 1.10x Rome

   5) The Mexica Triple Alliance, 1500
      A large, dense, literate, well-administered state with monumental
      construction, chinampa agriculture that outyields anything in Europe, and no
      draught animals, no iron, no wheel in practical use.
      5,000,000 people   state capacity 0.80   prices 0.80x Rome

==============================================================================
                      ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING THEY KNOW                    
==============================================================================

   You are one person, dropped into a pre-industrial society, carrying the
   knowledge of how modern technology works and none of the industry that makes
   it. Knowing how a thing works is free. Building it is not: it costs your own
   hours, other people's hours, money, materials, and years you do not get
   back.

   You arrive alone. No employees, no slaves, nobody who owes you anything, and
   about enough money to eat for a few months.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHERE, AND WHEN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   1) The Later Han Empire, 100
      Rome's exact contemporary and ahead of it in metallurgy, agriculture and
      bureaucracy. Cast iron for five centuries already, the seed drill, the
      moldboard plough, paper in the year 105, water-powered blast bellows in 31
      AD.
      58,000,000 people   state capacity 0.90   prices 0.75x Rome

   2) The Roman Empire under Trajan, 100
      Peak territorial extent, sound currency, superb civil engineering, an
      economy resting on slavery, and an elite that despises manual work.
      65,000,000 people   state capacity 0.85   prices 1.00x Rome

   3) Scandinavia in the Viking age, 900
      Small population, no state to speak of, superb shipbuilding and ironworking,
      and the best long-range mobility in Europe. The opposite problem from Rome:
      nobody will stop you, and nobody can fund you either.
      1,500,000 people   state capacity 0.15   prices 1.40x Rome

   4) England under Edward I, 1300
      Watermills and windmills everywhere, a real legal system, chartered towns,
      universities, the horse collar, the crank, the mechanical clock arriving,
      and about to be hit by the worst demographic catastrophe in European
      history.
      4,500,000 people   state capacity 0.60   prices 1.10x Rome

   5) The Mexica Triple Alliance, 1500
      A large, dense, literate, well-administered state with monumental
      construction, chinampa agriculture that outyields anything in Europe, and no
      draught animals, no iron, no wheel in practical use.
      5,000,000 people   state capacity 0.80   prices 0.80x Rome

   Which one? [1-5, or q to leave] 
==============================================================================
   SCANDINAVIA IN THE VIKING AGE, 900
==============================================================================

   You come ashore somewhere on the Vestfold, in a country with no king worth
   the name, no cities, no coinage anybody trusts, and no state to ask
   permission from. There are perhaps a million and a half people in the whole
   of Scandinavia. Every one of them is somebody's neighbour, and the law is an
   assembly of free men who will hear you.

   WHAT YOU CAN SEE
   The best ships in the world. Clinker-built, sprung, shallow enough for a
   river and sound enough for an ocean, and the men who build them do it by
   eye. Iron smelted from bog ore in every valley. Wool, tar, timber, and a
   trade network that reaches Baghdad in one direction and Newfoundland in the
   other.

   WHAT IS MISSING
   Everything that needs a state. There is no one to fund a public work, no
   city to concentrate a trade in, no bureaucracy to keep a record for longer
   than a man's memory. What Rome finds trivial, you will find nearly
   impossible. What Rome finds impossible, you can simply do, because nobody
   here can stop you.

   WHAT IS COMING, AND ONLY YOU KNOW IT
   A century of Christianisation and consolidation. Kings, bishops, written
   law, taxes and towns. The freedom you are enjoying now is the thing that is
   about to end.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   FOG OF WAR. With it on you see what you have built, what you could begin
   today as a one-line summary, and things you have heard of but cannot yet
   start. You cannot see where anything leads. With it off you can see the
   whole tree and plan a route through it.

   Fog of war? [Y/n] 
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHAT YOU ARRIVED WITH
      destitute              0 den
         the clothes you stand in. You must earn your first meal.
      poor_scholar         400 den
         DEFAULT. A few months' subsistence, a knife, a lens, a codex of notes. About
         what a working teacher has.
      artisan            1,200 den
         enough to rent a workshop and buy a first set of tools.
      merchant           4,000 den
         a modest trading capital. You can fund one real venture.
      rich_merchant     20,000 den
         wealthy but well under the equestrian census of 100,000.
      equestrian       100,000 den
         the equestrian census exactly. Conspicuous.
      absurd         1,000,000 den
         four senatorial fortunes in unminted gold. It used to make things worse and
         no longer does: once money can be converted into protection and into sunk
         mines, wealth helps. What it does NOT do is make you a magician: a million
         denarii buys perhaps a tenth off the time, not a different game. What money
         changes most is the OPENING - the first fifty years, where a poor founder is
         choosing between eating and building.

   Which? [destitute/poor_scholar/artisan/merchant/rich_merchant/equestrian/absurd]

   whole game is that one is the honest number.

changed:
  auto open: True
what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay. Mostly craftsmen, because craftsmen are what keep concerns open; some scholars; and it replaces any trade you taught as its people die off. It spends only a share of your surplus, so with no surplus it hires nobody
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.
switched on but cannot act right now:
  auto open: nothing to open with: opening a concern costs stock and premises

[932 AD | 1914 hacksilver | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 4 | rep 55] > Found the school (the Museum)  [school_founded]
===============================================
tier 1, institution, confidence C

The pivot of the entire game. Converts your hours into other people's hours
permanently. Every year of delay here costs more than any single technology.
Grants +4 scholars and +2 scholars/yr thereafter. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by
diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to
train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy
this down. OPTIONAL. Nothing in the technical tree requires it. It is simply
the highest-leverage thing you can spend money on, because it converts your
hours into other people's hours permanently. You may decline to found it and
hire craftsmen forever instead; the simulator will let you, and will show
you the cost.

[932 AD | 1914 hacksilver | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 4 | rep 55] > Buy, train and manumit a technical staff  [freedman_staff]
==========================================================
tier 1, institution, confidence C

Acquire, train and free a technical staff: buy or bind skilled workers,
teach them, release them from their obligation, then pay and keep them. A
freed worker who remains literate and paid transmits knowledge onward; a
coerced one does not. In Rome this is manumission of skilled slaves, who
retain an obligation to their former owner as patron and ran much of Roman
commerce; the Norse equivalent is working off a debt-thrall's bond.
Whichever form bondage takes where you are playing, this is both the ethical
and the efficient answer. Grants +8 artisans.

COST: 15,400 hacksilver total  (0 labour + 8,000 materials + 2,000 capital, then x1.1 your civ, x1 distance, x1 scarcity, x1 opposition, x1.4 prices)

                      ONE PERSON, AND EVERYTHING THEY KNOW                    
==============================================================================

   You are one person, dropped into a pre-industrial society, carrying the
   knowledge of how modern technology works and none of the industry that makes
   it. Knowing how a thing works is free. Building it is not: it costs your own
   hours, other people's hours, money, materials, and years you do not get
   back.

   You arrive alone. No employees, no slaves, nobody who owes you anything, and
   about enough money to eat for a few months.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
   WHERE, AND WHEN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

   1) The Later Han Empire, 100
      Rome's exact contemporary and ahead of it in metallurgy, agriculture and
      bureaucracy. Cast iron for five centuries already, the seed drill, the
      moldboard plough, paper in the year 105, water-powered blast bellows in 31
      AD.
      58,000,000 people   state capacity 0.90   prices 0.75x Rome

   2) The Roman Empire under Trajan, 100
      Peak territorial extent, sound currency, superb civil engineering, an
      economy resting on slavery, and an elite that despises manual work.
      65,000,000 people   state capacity 0.85   prices 1.00x Rome

   3) Scandinavia in the Viking age, 900
      Small population, no state to speak of, superb shipbuilding and ironworking,
      and the best long-range mobility in Europe. The opposite problem from Rome:
      nobody will stop you, and nobody can fund you either.
      1,500,000 people   state capacity 0.15   prices 1.40x Rome

   4) England under Edward I, 1300
      Watermills and windmills everywhere, a real legal system, chartered towns,
      universities, the horse collar, the crank, the mechanical clock arriving,
      and about to be hit by the worst demographic catastrophe in European
      history.
      4,500,000 people   state capacity 0.60   prices 1.10x Rome

   5) The Mexica Triple Alliance, 1500
      A large, dense, literate, well-administered state with monumental
      construction, chinampa agriculture that outyields anything in Europe, and no
      draught animals, no iron, no wheel in practical use.
      5,000,000 people   state capacity 0.80   prices 0.80x Rome

   Which one? [1-5, or q to leave] 
==============================================================================
   THE LATER HAN EMPIRE, 100
==============================================================================

   You arrive in Luoyang under the Emperor He, in a capital of timber and tile
   laid out on a grid, in the richest and most populous state on earth. There
   is a civil service recruited by examination, a standing bureaucracy that
   keeps records you can consult, and an imperial workshop system that already
   does things Rome cannot.

   WHAT YOU CAN SEE
   Cast iron, five hundred years before the West. The blast furnace. Paper,
   this very decade, credited to Cai Lun. The seed drill, the moldboard plough,
   the horse collar, the crossbow lock made to interchangeable tolerances, the
   seismoscope. A society that already believes in the trained specialist.

   WHAT IS MISSING
   Glass. The Han have almost none, and will not develop it: the whole optical
   branch that Rome could reach in a generation is, here, a thing you must
   start from sand and a furnace and an argument.

   WHAT IS COMING, AND ONLY YOU KNOW IT
   Eighty years, then the Yellow Turbans, then the warlords, then three
   centuries of division. The bureaucracy that makes this the easiest place on
   earth to organise anything is about to be the thing that breaks.

   today as a one-line summary, and things you have heard of but cannot yet
   start. You cannot see where anything leads. With it off you can see the
   whole tree and plan a route through it.

  auto hire: False

  auto mine: False
  auto forest: False
  auto mothball: True
  auto shed: False
  auto open: True
  auto commission: False
  auto bribe: False
changed:
  auto open: True
what each does:
  auto hire: grow the staff toward what you can house and pay. Mostly craftsmen, because craftsmen are what keep concerns open; some scholars; and it replaces any trade you taught as its people die off. It spends only a share of your surplus, so with no surplus it hires nobody
  auto buy people: buy slaves when the workshop is short-handed
  auto manumit: free people you hold, over time
  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

Alexandria (dry, preserves papyrus), a western site, an eastern site. The

defence and it is not optional. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by

across several provinces is precisely what Roman government fears: a
faction. Trajan refuses Pliny even a licensed fire brigade at Nicomedia for
this reason (Ep. 10.34). You need senatorial or imperial cover before you
attempt it, and you should site the three houses under three different
patrons so that it does not look like one organisation.

[141 AD | 983250 cash | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 18 | rep 94] > Found the school (the Museum)  [school_founded]
===============================================
tier 1, institution, confidence C

The pivot of the entire game. Converts your hours into other people's hours
permanently. Every year of delay here costs more than any single technology.
Grants +4 scholars and +2 scholars/yr thereafter. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by
diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to
train the trades, form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy
this down. OPTIONAL. Nothing in the technical tree requires it. It is simply
the highest-leverage thing you can spend money on, because it converts your
hours into other people's hours permanently. You may decline to found it and
hire craftsmen forever instead; the simulator will let you, and will show
you the cost.

COST: 8,625 cash total  (2,000 labour + 0 materials + 8,000 capital, then x1 your civ, x1 distance, x1 scarcity, x1.15 opposition, x0.75 prices)
YOUR HOURS: 2,000     CALENDAR FLOOR: 4 years     FAILURE RISK: 15%

[141 AD | 983250 cash | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 18 | rep 94] > Three geographically separated academies  [academy_network]
===========================================================
tier 3, institution, confidence C

Alexandria (dry, preserves papyrus), a western site, an eastern site. The
Third Century Crisis will destroy at least one. Redundancy is the only
defence and it is not optional. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by
construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to train the trades,
form the capital and build the suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. THE
STATE WILL ACTIVELY RESIST THIS. A large private association operating
across several provinces is precisely what Roman government fears: a
faction. Trajan refuses Pliny even a licensed fire brigade at Nicomedia for
this reason (Ep. 10.34). You need senatorial or imperial cover before you
attempt it, and you should site the three houses under three different
patrons so that it does not look like one organisation.

[141 AD | 983250 cash | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 18 | rep 94] > Endow the institute in land, not coin  [endowment_land]
=======================================================
tier 2, institution, confidence B

Land outlives coin: whatever currency you are using will eventually be
debased or disrupted, and land will not. This is how a programme outlives
its founder. In Rome the vehicle is testamentary law and the fundatio
(Pliny's alimenta, Trajan's own); every society you can play has some
durable equivalent, and it is bought or built the way endowments are always
built here: with a public benefaction and the right friends.

[141 AD | 983250 cash | you:2000 hr | sch 1 art 18 | rep 94] > Print and disperse hundreds of copies across three continents  [corpus_dispersed]
==============================================================================
tier 2, information, confidence C

THE highest expected-value node in the tree, and it is cheap. The lesson of
Alexandria is not that books burn, it is that single copies burn. Push
copies into every library, temple archive and private collection from
Britain to India. This is what carries the programme through 235-284 AD.
CALENDAR FLOOR is set by diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs
roughly a generation to train the trades, form the capital and build the
suppliers. Money cannot buy this down. Same objection as the press,
multiplied. Hundreds of copies of a technical corpus in private hands is
exactly what an anxious regime dislikes. Present it as a gift to the
libraries of the Empire and give the first copies to the emperor's own
foundations.

  auto train: teach trades this society does not have when a project needs them
  auto mine: sink a mine when a mineral is holding work up
  auto forest: buy coppice when charcoal is holding work up
  auto mothball: stop working mines you cannot pay for
  auto bribe: pay your way out of a scandal before it kills you
  auto shed: let go of WORKS that cost more than they return (this is about buildings and practices, not people)
  auto open: open concerns that plainly pay for themselves. It will NOT open anything whose upkeep exceeds its takings, however much you need it - open those yourself with 'open <id>'
note: Anything switched off here you can still do by hand: hire, train, buy, commission, mothball, restore, bribe.
not policies: Some things are consequences, not automation, and there is no switch for them: people you cannot pay leave, mines you cannot pay for stop being worked once your credit is gone, and creditors take what they are owed. Those follow from having no money, not from a setting.

[IN PROGRESS] The Sixteen Kingdoms
  A hundred and twenty years in which northern China was ruled by a rapid
  succession of short-lived states founded by Xiongnu, Jie, Xianbei, Di and
  Qiang rulers - conventionally sixteen, in fact rather more. Fu Jian's Former
  Qin came within one battle of reunifying everything and lost it in an
  afternoon at the Fei river in 383. Registered population in the north over
  this period is a small fraction of the Later Han totals; how much of that
  gap is death and how much is flight south and households that simply stopped
  being counted is disputed, which is why this is modelled as long sustained
  lost output and a low standing sack risk rather than as mass mortality. What
  is not disputed is that the thing that made Han China the easiest place in
  this game to organise anything - one court, one coinage, one set of
  examinations - is gone, and what replaces it is a warlord whose favour you
  either have or do not.
  sack chance: you take 85% of it (softened by land nobody can carry away)
    what would help: walls, firearms, powerful friends, and copies of your work kept somewhere else
    you could begin now: gunpowder (4,780, corned powder), mil_artillery_piece (6,798, a step toward angled bastion walls no ram or ladder answers)
    academy_network is one of them, waiting on: needs 10 trained scholars, you have 4.8 (you are one of them)
    mil_bastion is one of them, waiting on: missing prerequisites: mil_trace_italienne
  output factor: you take 34% of it (softened by land that yields whoever is emperor this year, you feed yourself, power that does not come by ship, your own roads, losses spread rather than borne)
  sack chance after what you have built: 2%
[439-534] Northern Wei, the equal-field system, and the monasteries
  The Tuoba Wei finished off the last of the northern states in 439 and held
  the north for a century. The equal-field allotment of 485 and the
  three-elders village registration of 486 rebuilt a taxable peasantry out of
  the wreckage, and Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang in 494 and
  required Xianbei families to take Chinese dress, language and surnames. The
  part that matters for a workshop is the Buddhist establishment: Yungang from
  460 and Longmen from 493 are the visible end of it, but the monasteries were
  also very large landholders that ran water-powered grain mills and oil
  presses on their estates and litigated to keep the water rights. That is an
  institutional home for machinery, with capital and a reason to want it, that
  Han China did not have. The cost side is that the state notices: Emperor
  Taiwu suppressed Buddhism in 446 and the Northern Zhou did it again from 574
  to 577, forcibly returning something like three million monks and nuns and
  their land to the tax rolls, which is a state deciding what may be believed
  in a way the Later Han rarely did.

[569 AD | 79147660 cash | you:18324 hr | sch 15 art 278 | rep 78] > Zinc smelting at industrial scale, with flue dust collection  [zinc_industry_scale]
==============================================================================
tier 5, metallurgy, confidence B

Zinc is the hidden gate on the electrical age and this node is 83 per cent
of the whole tree's charcoal. The carbon here does two jobs, reducing the
oxide inside the retort and firing the retort from outside, and coke serves
for both: the Belgian horizontal retorts ran on coal. That matters
enormously, because 54,000 tonnes of charcoal a year is 72,000 hectares of
coppice, and coal you can dig. Zinc earns its own way as brass, galvanising
and batteries. Its second and hidden purpose is that germanium concentrates
in the flue dust of zinc smelters, at the parts-per-thousand level in the
dust against 1.6 ppm in the crust. Design the flues for dust collection from
the first furnace or you will rebuild them later. CALENDAR FLOOR is set by
diffusion, not by construction: the economy needs roughly a generation to

[569 AD | 79147660 cash | you:18324 hr | sch 15 art 278 | rep 78] > Germanium concentrate from flue dust and coal ash  [germanium_extraction]
=========================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence B

Germanium is 1.6 ppm in the crust and essentially never occurs as its own
workable ore in reach. Zinc flue dust and certain coal ashes are the
realistic sources. The spectroscope is how you find it at all: without

ever seen.

[569 AD | 79147660 cash | you:18324 hr | sch 15 art 278 | rep 78] > Germanium tetrachloride fractional distillation  [gecl4_purification]
=====================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

The door. Germanium is a nightmare to purify as metal or oxide and easy as a
volatile chloride boiling at about 86 C, which you can fractionate like
brandy. Distil repeatedly in a tall packed column, hydrolyse back to the
dioxide with ultrapure water, and you are already at parts per million
before you have done anything clever.

[569 AD | 79147660 cash | you:18324 hr | sch 15 art 278 | rep 78] > Zone refining to one part in 1e9  [zone_refining]
=================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

The specific trick that makes semiconductors possible at all. Most
impurities prefer the liquid, so a narrow molten zone dragged along an ingot
sweeps them to one end; repeat and the purity compounds. Nothing else
reaches these levels. It needs a tube furnace, a quartz or graphite boat, a
hydrogen or inert atmosphere, and a way to move a heater slowly and
repeatably, which is why it waits on motors.

[569 AD | 79147660 cash | you:18324 hr | sch 15 art 278 | rep 78] > Czochralski single crystal growth and controlled doping  [single_crystal]
=========================================================================
tier 5, semiconductor, confidence A

Dip a seed into the melt and pull slowly while rotating. Grain boundaries
destroy carrier lifetime, so polycrystalline germanium will never make a
working transistor no matter how pure it is. Add the dopant to the melt in
weighed traces; this is where the analytical balance earns its keep two
centuries later.
